items.d: A **dilemma** is a choice between **two rights** (loyalty to the institution versus transparency to the public); a **temptation** is a choice between **right and wrong** dressed up as a dilemma. Naming which one the case is — and refusing to treat a temptation as a dilemma — is the single highest-scoring move in a Section B answer.

**Truth versus loyalty · individual versus community · short term versus long term · justice versus mercy**. Kidder's three resolution principles: **ends-based (utilitarian), rule-based (Kantian) and care-based (do as you would be done by)**. Naming the paradigm converts a narrative answer into an analytical one.
items.s: Rushworth Kidder, How Good People Make Tough Choices

items.d: A situation where a public servant's **private interest could improperly influence** the discharge of official duty — actual, apparent or potential. The remedy sequence is **disclose → recuse → divest**, and 'apparent' matters as much as 'actual' because public trust turns on perception.

**Integrity** is the alignment of conduct with values even when unobserved; **probity** adds the procedural dimension — uprightness in the use of public funds and authority. The Second ARC's **'Ethics in Governance'** report is the standard citation; the **Nolan Committee's Seven Principles of Public Life** (selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership) are the standard list.

**Moral courage** is acting on conviction despite risk of loss — distinct from physical courage. **Moral injury** is the lasting damage from being made to act against one's own moral code, or from witnessing it without being able to prevent it — the honest name for what long service under pressure does to an officer.

**Normative drift** — small deviations become the new normal because each is individually trivial; **ethical fading** — the moral dimension of a decision disappears from view once it is framed as a technical, legal or financial problem. Both explain how honest institutions decay without any single act of corruption.

Doing only what the rule strictly requires — 'it is not illegal' as the whole of the answer. The public servant's obligation runs to the **spirit of the rule and the public interest**, not the letter alone; the legal floor is a floor, not a ceiling.

**Relativism** — moral judgements are valid only within a culture; **absolutism** — some acts are wrong regardless of context. The workable position for a civil servant is **constitutional universalism**: the Constitution's values supply a non-negotiable floor while permitting contextual judgement above it.

**Goleman's five components** — self-awareness, self-regulation, motivation, empathy and social skill. In administration: empathy makes grievance redress meaningful, self-regulation prevents escalation in a crowd situation, and self-awareness is what makes conflict-of-interest disclosure possible at all.

**ABC model — Affective (feeling), Behavioural (action tendency), Cognitive (belief)**; attitudes are changed through persuasion (**Elaboration Likelihood Model — central and peripheral routes**), by resolving **cognitive dissonance (Festinger)**, or through contact. Applied use: Swachh Bharat and Beti Bachao are **attitude-change programmes**, which is why behavioural nudges outperformed construction targets.

**Thaler and Sunstein** — a nudge alters behaviour predictably **without forbidding options or significantly changing incentives**. Indian instances: the **'Give It Up' LPG subsidy campaign**, default enrolment in Atal Pension, the Economic Survey 2018-19's chapter on **'Nudge: from BBBP to BADLAV'**, and the toilet-usage campaigns.

Internal versus external disclosure; the ethical test is **the gravity of the wrong, the exhaustion of internal channels, the reliability of the evidence, and proportionality**. India's **Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 has never been brought into force** — the reason **Satyendra Dubey (NHAI, 2003)** and **Manjunath Shanmugam (IOC, 2005)** are cited as the cost of that gap.

**Responsibility** is the obligation to perform; **accountability** is the obligation to answer for performance to someone with the power to sanction. The **'many hands' problem** — where everyone is responsible, no one is accountable — is why file-noting, recorded oral instructions and single-point ownership matter.

The public servant holds authority and resources **in trust for the citizen**, not as owner — the duty of loyalty and the duty of care. It converts 'discretion' from a personal privilege into a trust obligation, and is the cleanest justification for recusal, disclosure and the public-trust doctrine.

groups.g: Ethics in governance and public service

items.d: **Integrity, impartiality, non-partisanship, objectivity, dedication to public service, empathy, tolerance and compassion towards the weaker sections** — the values the Second ARC recommended be given statutory form in a **Public Services Bill**, and which the **draft Public Service Code** lists. Add **anonymity and political neutrality** from the Westminster tradition.

items.t: Codes of conduct and codes of ethics
items.d: A **code of conduct** is prescriptive and enumerative — the **All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968** and the **CCS (Conduct) Rules, 1964**: no acceptance of gifts beyond limits, prior sanction for acquiring property, restrictions on criticism of government, no participation in politics. A **code of ethics** is aspirational and value-based. India is **conduct-rule heavy and ethics-code light** — the Second ARC's core criticism.

**CVC (statutory, 2003)**, **CBI (DSPE Act, 1946)**, **Lokpal and Lokayuktas Act, 2013**, **PC Act, 1988 (amended 2018)**, **RTI Act, 2005**, **Prevention of Money Laundering Act, 2002**, the **Benami Transactions Act**, **Citizens' Charters**, **social audit**, and the **Integrity Pact** (a Transparency International instrument) used in defence and large public procurement.

**Petty versus grand**; **collusive versus coercive** (collusive is more damaging because there is no complainant); **extortionary**; **quid pro quo versus 'speed money'**; **state capture**; and the distinction between **corruption of process and corruption of outcome**. The Second ARC's phrase — corruption is **'a low-risk, high-reward activity'** — states the incentive problem in one line.

**Corporate governance** (Kotak Committee, SEBI LODR, independent directors, related-party transactions); **CSR under Section 135** — India as the first country to mandate it; **ESG reporting (BRSR)**; and **professional ethics** — the distinction between the **client model, the agency model and the fiduciary model** of the professional's obligation.

**Algorithmic bias and explainability**, **surveillance and the proportionality test from *Puttaswamy***, **informed consent and data minimisation under the DPDP Act**, **deepfakes and synthetic media**, **the digital divide as an exclusion risk in DBT authentication**, and the **precautionary principle applied to AI**. India's **Responsible AI principles (NITI Aayog, 2021)**: safety and reliability, equality, inclusivity and non-discrimination, privacy and security, transparency, accountability, and protection of positive human values.
items.s: NITI Aayog, Responsible AI for All

items.d: **Anthropocentrism** (nature as instrument) versus **biocentrism/ecocentrism** (intrinsic worth of all life — the basis of granting rights to rivers, as the Uttarakhand HC did for the Ganga and Yamuna in 2017); **deep ecology (Arne Naess)**; **intergenerational equity**; and Gandhi's **'enough for every man's need, not every man's greed'**. The **Chipko** and **Bishnoi** traditions supply the Indian instances.

**Common but differentiated responsibilities**, the ethics of **climate finance and loss and damage**, **vaccine equity** (India's Vaccine Maitri, 300+ million doses to 100+ countries), **humanitarian intervention versus sovereignty (R2P)**, and **ethics in international trade** — TRIPS flexibilities and compulsory licensing (India's *Natco v. Bayer* licence for Nexavar, 2012) as the balance between patent rights and the right to health.
